1. Introduction: Purpose of the Work

Uncollected loans have historically been one of the primary challenges facing banks and financial institutions, representing a significant source of financial loss. While these businesses profit considerably from interest on loans, they must also bear substantial costs when borrowers fail to repay their debts. These defaults not only strain profitability but also impact operational stability and long-term growth. Addressing this issue has become critical for maintaining financial health and improving lending strategies.

The objective of this work is to build a predictive model to assist banks in mitigating losses associated with uncollected loans. By leveraging historical data, the model aims to predict the likelihood of loan repayment, enabling better decision-making in loan approvals and risk management. With a robust predictive system, banks can improve internal financial planning, reduce exposure to high-risk borrowers, and optimize resource allocation for loan recovery efforts.

The dataset used in this analysis comes from an American financial services business, spanning the period from April 2008 to September 2015. Among its many features, the dataset includes a key variable, loan_status, which indicates the repayment status of each loan. Using this and other attributes, the model will help predict whether loans will be repaid or defaulted. This tool not only aids in reducing potential losses but also empowers the company to develop more informed and effective lending policies.

In summary, this report aims to provide a data-driven solution for a pressing issue in the banking sector by building a predictive model for loan analysis. The insights derived from this work will help the business enhance its financial resilience and support better credit risk assessment practices.

b. Pre-processing the data


Converting the Target Variable

As mentioned, the target variable is the loan_status of each customer, but as we can see below, there are some of these categories that should be disregarded considering the goal of prediction if the loan is delayed or not.

levels(df$loan_status)
##  [1] "Charged Off"                                        
##  [2] "Current"                                            
##  [3] "Default"                                            
##  [4] "Does not meet the credit policy. Status:Charged Off"
##  [5] "Does not meet the credit policy. Status:Fully Paid" 
##  [6] "Fully Paid"                                         
##  [7] "In Grace Period"                                    
##  [8] "Issued"                                             
##  [9] "Late (16-30 days)"                                  
## [10] "Late (31-120 days)"

To ensure the analysis is focused and aligned with the objective of predicting whether loans will be collected or not, certain loan statuses and categories will be excluded from the dataset. Specifically, loans categorized as Does not meet the credit policy. Status: Fully Paid and Does not meet the credit policy. Status: Charged Off will be removed, as these do not align with the credit policy criteria under consideration. Additionally, loans currently In Grace Period and those classified as Issued will also be excluded, as they are not actively in the repayment phase and do not provide relevant information for the binary prediction task.

By narrowing the dataset to include only loans that meet the credit policy and are within the payment period, the analysis can focus on predicting loan repayment outcomes effectively. This approach ensures the predictive model is built on a dataset representative of the target scenario, thereby enhancing its reliability and applicability in assessing whether loans will be collected or not.

The following code deletes the rows in which the column loan_status is one of the levels we decided to drop:

df <- df[!df$loan_status %in% c("In Grace Period",
                                "Issued",
                                "Does not meet the credit policy. Status:Charged Off", 
                                "Does not meet the credit policy. Status:Fully Paid"), ]


Creating the Target Variable:

With the loan_status variable appropriately cleaned, we can now create a binary target variable, y. This variable consolidates all “positive” loan statuses into a single positive group and all “negative” loan statuses into a single negative group. By transforming the data into a binary format, the predictive model becomes more straightforward to interpret and implement.

This approach aligns with the primary objective of the analysis: to predict whether a loan will be repaid or not. The binary classification simplifies the predictive process and provides a clear and actionable output for decision-making. By focusing on this streamlined prediction, the model delivers practical insights that support the bank’s goal of efficiently assessing credit risk and optimizing its lending strategy.

df$y <- ifelse(df$loan_status %in% c("Charged Off", "Default", "Late (31-120 days)"), 0, 1)
str(df$y)
##  num [1:869917] 1 0 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 0 ...

As seen, the code below creates a new column y on the dataset. Now the target variable is a binary, numeric column.

Deleting Columns:

Meaningless Columns:

Certain columns, such as id, prime_id, and url, are excluded from the dataset as they hold no predictive power and do not contribute to the modeling process. These columns are essentially identifiers or metadata that are irrelevant to the prediction task and could introduce noise if retained.

In addition to these non-informative columns, the loan_status variable is also removed. Since y (the binary target variable) is derived directly from loan_status, the latter is inherently redundant and would create perfect multicollinearity if included in the analysis. Retaining it could compromise the integrity of the predictive model by introducing circular reasoning, where the target variable is predicted using itself. To ensure the model’s reliability and validity, loan_status is excluded from the predictors.

df <- df[, !names(df) %in% c('loan_status', 'url', 'id', 'member_id')]
#str(df)


Future Variables:

Future variables refer to data that would not be available at the time of making the prediction, such as information about loan repayment or behaviors occurring after the loan is issued. Including these variables can lead to data leakage, where the model uses information it wouldn’t have in real-world scenarios, resulting in overly optimistic performance during training but poor generalization to new data. To prevent this, future variables must be excluded during data pre-processing to ensure the model is trained only on features realistically available at the time of prediction, making it both valid and reliable for practical use.

Here we delete those:

df <- df[, !names(df) %in% c('grade', 'sub_grade','pymnt_plan', 'funded_amnt_inv')]
#str(df)

df[df == ""] <- NA
df[df == "n/a"] <- NA

Given the substantial number of predictive columns in the dataset, we opted to remove any columns with more than 10% missing values. When the proportion of missing data is too high, imputation methods become less reliable and may introduce unnecessary bias into the dataset. By excluding these columns, we aim to preserve the integrity of the analysis and ensure the predictive model is built on robust and trustworthy data.

df <- df[, na_percentage <= threshold]

For the numerical variables, the initial plan was to replace missing values with the column’s median, as this is a common and robust imputation method. However, this approach can still introduce some degree of bias into the dataset. Given the large number of observations available, we determined that the potential risk of bias outweighs the benefit of retaining rows with missing values. Instead, we opted to remove rows with missing numerical values, as this approach ensures data integrity while still leaving a sufficient number of observations to build reliable and effective predictive models.

df <- df %>%
  filter(across(where(is.numeric), ~ !is.na(.)))
#str(df)

For the categorical variables, rather than deleting rows with missing values, we opted to create a new category labeled “Unknown.” This approach retains all observations while preserving the dataset’s completeness, ensuring that no potentially valuable information is lost. By assigning missing values to the “Unknown” category, we can account for their presence in the analysis without introducing bias or distortion, allowing the predictive model to handle these cases effectively.

df <- df %>%
  mutate(across(c("emp_title", "emp_length", "title", "last_pymnt_d", "last_credit_pull_d"), ~ ifelse(is.na(.), "Unkown", .)))

# the function above transformed these columns into characters, sowe are just going to transform back to factors
df <- df %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

To ensure that all missing values have been properly handled, the following code snippet counts the NA values across the entire dataset:

final_missing_values <- sum(is.na(df))
cat("Total missing values in the dataset:", final_missing_values, "\n")
## Total missing values in the dataset: 0


Addressing factor columns with too many levels:

For models such as Logistic Regression, KNN, ANN, and SVM, the data needs to be encoded or dummified (a process explained later). This involves creating a separate column for each level of every categorical variable. However, some factors in the dataset have an excessively high number of levels, which can make the models computationally expensive and inefficient.

To address this, we decided to set these high-cardinality variables to NULL, effectively excluding them from the analysis. While these variables may have some predictive power, the dataset contains sufficient remaining predictors to build accurate models without them. It is worth noting that in scenarios where computational power is not a limitation, this step could be skipped, and all variables could be included for a potentially more comprehensive analysis.

df$emp_title <- NULL
df$title <- NULL
df$issue_d  <- NULL
df$addr_state <- NULL
df$zip_code <- NULL
df$earliest_cr_line <- NULL
df$last_pymnt_d <- NULL
df$last_credit_pull_d <- NULL


Getting a random sample of 10% of the dataset:

After addressing the dataset’s issues and ensuring it is properly treated, we decided to proceed with a random sample of 10% of the rows from the dataset. This step was introduced to accommodate current computational limitations, ensuring the modeling process remains efficient and manageable. However, it is important to note that in scenarios where computational resources are not a constraint, this step can be entirely skipped, allowing the full dataset to be utilized for potentially more robust model training.

Here, we considered creating a balanced random sample, consisting of 50% random samples from negative cases (defaulted loans) and 50% random samples from positive cases (repaid loans). While this approach could potentially improve the performance of models that struggle with imbalanced datasets, we decided against it. Balancing the dataset artificially could misrepresent the actual distribution of the target variable and complicate the model’s predictions on new, real-world data, where the distribution will remain imbalanced. By retaining the original distribution, we ensure the model’s performance and predictions remain realistic and applicable to the actual business context.

sample_size <- 0.1
set.seed(12345)
sample_rows <- sample(1:nrow(df), sample_size*nrow(df))
sample_data <- df[sample_rows, ]
#str(sample_data)


Encoding Categorical Variables:

As mentioned earlier, most of the models we will be using cannot handle categorical columns with more than two levels (i.e., non-binary categorical variables). To address this, we encode the dataset to transform these categorical variables into a format that the models can process effectively.

This encoding process, known as dummification or one-hot encoding, converts each level of a categorical variable into its own separate column. For example, the home_ownership variable is transformed into new columns such as ANY, MORTGAGE, OWN, etc., with each row indicating the presence or absence of a specific level. Importantly, the encoding process excludes one column for each factor, which prevents issues with multicollinearity by avoiding redundant information. This ensures the dataset is both interpretable and compatible with the predictive models we are implementing.

encoded_data <- as.data.frame(model.matrix(~ . -1, sample_data))
#str(encoded_data)
#summary(encoded_data)

# To make the term 36/60 months without " "
colnames(encoded_data) <- make.names(colnames(encoded_data))

# Delete cuz is either all 0 or all 1s
encoded_data$purposeeducational <- NULL
encoded_data$policy_code <- NULL


Scaling Numerical Variables: remember to adjust text based on SVM

Finally, the last step of cleaning is scaling our data. Further on in our analysis, we will build models such as a KNN and a ANN; for these models, our numeric factors have to be comparable to one another. For this to happen, they have to be on the same scale, so we create a separate variable that contains scaled data for the those models. We utilize min max scaling in this instance, so each numeric variable is now on a scale of 0-1.

minmax <- function(x) {
  (x - min(x)) / (max(x)-min(x))
}
scaled_data <- as.data.frame(lapply(encoded_data, minmax))

While understanding these steps is not essential from a business perspective, it is important to note that the data has been thoroughly cleaned and prepared to ensure the analysis is accurate, reliable, and aligned with the project’s objectives.

3. Unsupervised Learning


Once with the data cleaned and pre-processed, and the analysis of the current scenario concluded, we are ready to start with the unsupervised learning.

Business Note: This segment focuses on building seven prediction models—Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbors, Neural Network, Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost—to identify potential loan defaults. The goal is to determine if avoiding high-risk loans based on predictions can deliver better financial outcomes compared to the current approach.

a. Split the data

Data splitting is essential in model training as it enables us to evaluate a model’s performance on data it hasn’t encountered before. By dividing our data into training and test sets, we create two separate groups: one for training the model (the training set) and another for evaluating its performance (the test set). This method helps us avoid overfitting, where the model could learn the training data too well and struggle to generalize to new, unseen data.

In this setup, we use a test split rate of 0.5, dividing the dataset equally into 50% training and 50% testing for each model configuration. Given the large number of rows in the dataset, allocating half for training is sufficient to ensure robust model development while leaving ample data for testing. This approach provides a reliable basis for evaluating model performance and enables firmer analysis and comparison of financial results in the end of this report (as the test set is bigger). Moreover, the 50-50 split reduces computational demands for heavier models like Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) and Support Vector Machines (SVM), ensuring the modeling process remains efficient without compromising accuracy or insights.

Also, we did separate splits for network models vs. the rest of them. We sample rows from the scaled_data dataset to create training and test sets for the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), while for all the other models we are splitting the encoded_data dataset, in which the data was not scaled.

Scaling the dataset is crucial for models like K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) because these algorithms are sensitive to the magnitude of the input features. In KNN, the distance between data points determines their classification or prediction, and unscaled data can give undue weight to features with larger numerical ranges. Similarly, ANN models rely on gradient-based optimization, where unscaled inputs can lead to inefficient or biased training due to larger feature values dominating the gradients. In contrast, models such as Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines (SVM), Decision Trees, Random Forest, and XGBoost do not require scaling. Logistic Regression can handle unscaled data as it estimates probabilities directly. SVM uses kernel functions, and tree-based methods (Decision Trees, Random Forest, XGBoost) split data based on feature thresholds, which are scale-independent. Therefore, scaling is only necessary for KNN and ANN to ensure optimal performance, while it can be omitted for the other models.

test_rate <- 0.5
set.seed(12345)

test_rows <- sample(1:nrow(sample_data), test_rate*nrow(sample_data))
train_data <- sample_data[-test_rows, ]
test_data <- sample_data[test_rows, ]

# Log Regression, SVM, Decision Tree, Random Forest - Encoded
train_encoded <- encoded_data[-test_rows, ]
test_encoded <- encoded_data[test_rows, ]

# KNN, ANN Split - Encoded and Scaled
train_scaled <- scaled_data[-test_rows, ]
test_scaled <- scaled_data[test_rows, ]


b. Logistic Regression Model

Logistic Regression is a statistical model used for binary classification tasks, where the goal is to predict one of two possible outcomes (e.g., yes/no, default/no default). It estimates the probability of an event occurring by modeling the relationship between one or more independent variables and a binary dependent variable. Logistic Regression uses a sigmoid function to map predicted values to probabilities between 0 and 1, and it applies a threshold (commonly 0.5) to classify observations into one of the two categories. It is widely used for its simplicity, interpretability, and effectiveness in understanding the impact of predictor variables on the target outcome.

log_regression <- glm(as.factor(y) ~ ., data = train_encoded, family = binomial)
prediction_lr <- predict(log_regression, test_encoded, type = "response")

#stepwise_lr <- step(log_regression, direction = "both", trace = 0)
#prediction_stepwise <- predict(stepwise_lr, test_encoded, type = "response")

binary_prediction_lr <- ifelse(prediction_lr < .25, 0, 1)

cm_lr <- confusionMatrix(as.factor(binary_prediction_lr),
                as.factor(test_encoded$y),
                positive = "1")
cm_lr

The confusion matrix for the Logistic Regression model provides the following insights:

  1. Accuracy: The model achieved an accuracy of 97.56%, which is very high. This indicates that the Logistic Regression model is effective at correctly classifying loan repayment outcomes.

  2. Kappa: The Kappa statistic is 0.752, showing substantial agreement between predicted and actual loan statuses, beyond what is expected by chance. This demonstrates good performance even with some degree of class imbalance.

  3. Sensitivity: The sensitivity is 99.42%, meaning the model performs exceptionally well in identifying loans that are likely to be repaid (positive class). This is crucial for minimizing false negatives.

  4. Specificity: The specificity is 67.68%, suggesting that the model has moderate success in identifying defaulted loans (negative class). While lower than sensitivity, it is still acceptable given the overall performance.

  5. Positive Predictive Value (PPV): The PPV is 98.02%, indicating that when the model predicts a loan will be repaid, it is correct the vast majority of the time. This is valuable for decision-making regarding loan approvals.

  6. Balanced Accuracy: The balanced accuracy, which averages sensitivity and specificity, is 83.55%, reflecting robust overall performance across both classes.

Overall, the Logistic Regression model demonstrates strong performance, with high accuracy and sensitivity ensuring that loans likely to be repaid are effectively identified. However, its specificity is relatively lower, highlighting a need for improvement in detecting defaulted loans. Despite this, the model remains a reliable tool for predicting loan repayment outcomes. The stepwise regression approach was again commented out due to computational demands and the satisfactory results of the simpler model.

c. KNN Model

The K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm is a non-parametric, instance-based machine learning model used for classification and regression tasks. For classification, it works by identifying the k closest data points (neighbors) to a query point in the feature space and assigning the majority class of those neighbors to the query. The model relies heavily on the concept of distance (commonly Euclidean) and is sensitive to feature scaling. KNN is simple, intuitive, and effective for datasets where the relationship between features and target labels is not well-defined by a mathematical function.

y_col <- which(colnames(train_scaled) == "y")
prediction_knn <- knn(train = train_scaled[,-y_col], 
                      test = test_scaled[,-y_col], 
                      cl = train_scaled[,y_col], 
                      k = 1) 
#summary(prediction_knn)

cm_knn <- confusionMatrix(as.factor(prediction_knn), as.factor(test_scaled$y), positive = "1")
cm_knn

Before the analysis of the results we wanted to explain the choice of the k. With a highly imbalanced dataset, the majority class dominates, and using a larger k could exacerbate this issue by allowing more majority-class neighbors to influence the classification decision. By setting k = 1, the model relies solely on the closest neighbor, which helps avoid amplifying the imbalance effect and allows the model to focus on the local behavior of individual data points.

The confusion matrix for the KNN model (k=1) provides the following insights:

  1. Accuracy: The model achieved an accuracy of 93.03%, which is good but slightly lower than the Logistic Regression model. This indicates that while the KNN model performs well overall, there is some room for improvement, particularly in handling the negative class.

  2. Kappa: The Kappa statistic is 0.2762, which reflects only fair agreement between predictions and actual values. This suggests that the model struggles to balance performance across the imbalanced classes.

  3. Sensitivity: The sensitivity is 97.13%, demonstrating that the model is highly effective at identifying loans that are likely to be repaid (positive class). This is critical for ensuring reliable predictions for the majority class.

  4. Specificity: The specificity is 27.04%, indicating that the model has significant difficulty identifying defaulted loans (negative class). This leads to a high number of false positives, highlighting the impact of the class imbalance.

  5. Positive Predictive Value (PPV): The PPV is 95.54%, meaning that when the model predicts a loan will be repaid, it is correct most of the time. This is beneficial for decision-making on loan approvals.

  6. Balanced Accuracy: The balanced accuracy, which averages sensitivity and specificity, is 62.08%, reflecting moderate overall performance, but the model is biased toward the majority class.

The KNN model with k=1 performs well in identifying loans likely to be repaid, as evidenced by its high sensitivity and PPV. However, it struggles to correctly classify defaulted loans, with low specificity and Kappa values. These weaknesses are likely due to the class imbalance and the use of k=1, which makes the model highly sensitive to local noise in the data. We attempted adjusting k to improve tis specificity, however, it did not work (likely due to the high imbalance already mentioned). Addressing the class imbalance (e.g., through resampling techniques) could improve the model’s performance in detecting the minority class, however we did not try to do it as we aim to use this regression on the stack model, and we need to maintain the same rows of train and test sets throughout all models to do so.

d. ANN Model

An Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is a machine learning model inspired by the structure and functioning of the human brain. It consists of layers of interconnected nodes (neurons) that process input data through weighted connections. ANNs excel at modeling complex, non-linear relationships in data by learning patterns through backpropagation, where weights are adjusted iteratively to minimize errors. They are particularly powerful for tasks like image recognition, natural language processing, and predictive modeling, offering flexibility and adaptability for a wide range of problems.

model_ann <- neuralnet(y ~ ., data = train_scaled, hidden = c(1), stepmax = 1e7, lifesign = "none", threshold = 0.1)
plot(model_ann)

prediction_ann <- predict(model_ann, newdata = test_scaled)
binary_prediction_ann <- ifelse(prediction_ann > 0.25, 1, 0)

cm_ann <- confusionMatrix(as.factor(binary_prediction_ann), as.factor(test_scaled$y))
cm_ann

e. SVM Model

A Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a powerful supervised machine learning model used for classification and regression tasks. It works by finding the optimal hyperplane that separates data points into distinct classes with the maximum margin. The margin is the distance between the hyperplane and the nearest data points from each class, known as support vectors. SVMs are versatile and can handle linear and non-linear relationships in data by using kernel functions, which map the input features into higher-dimensional spaces where classes become more separable. This flexibility, combined with its robustness to overfitting in high-dimensional spaces, makes SVMs highly effective for complex classification problems.

To identify the best-performing kernel for the Support Vector Machine (SVM) model, I implemented a function, try_kernels, that systematically tests various kernels and evaluates their performance. This function trains an SVM model using the specified kernel on the scaled training dataset (train_scaled) and generates predictions on the scaled test dataset (test_scaled). For each kernel, the function calculates and returns three key metrics from the confusion matrix: accuracy, kappa, and sensitivity. These metrics provide a comprehensive evaluation of the model’s performance, capturing overall correctness, agreement beyond chance, and the ability to identify positive cases.

The function is applied to a list of kernels (kernels), including “vanilladot”, “polydot”, “rbfdot”, “tanhdot”, “anovadot”, “laplacedot”, and “besseldot” using sapply to iterate over each kernel. This streamlined approach makes it easy to compare the results and select the most suitable kernel for the final SVM model based on performance metrics, ensuring optimal results for the analysis.

try_kernels <- function(kernel_name) {
  suppressMessages({
    model <- ksvm(as.factor(y) ~ ., data = train_scaled, kernel = kernel_name)
  })
  predictions <- predict(model, test_scaled)
  cm <- confusionMatrix(as.factor(predictions), as.factor(test_scaled$y), positive = "1")
  
  accuracy <- cm$overall["Accuracy"]
  kappa <- cm$overall["Kappa"]
  sensitivity <- cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]
  
  # Return all metrics
  return(c(accuracy = accuracy, kappa = kappa, sensitivity = sensitivity))
}

kernels <- c("vanilladot", "polydot", "rbfdot", "tanhdot", "anovadot", "laplacedot", "besseldot")
sapply(kernels, try_kernels)

Based on the results of the try_kernels function, the best kernel to apply to your SVM model is “vanilladot” (the linear kernel). Here’s why:

  1. Accuracy: The linear kernel (“vanilladot”) achieved an accuracy of 98.29%, which is the highest among all tested kernels (tied with “polydot” and slightly better than “anovadot”).

  2. Kappa: The Kappa statistic for the linear kernel is 0.8213, also the highest among the kernels. This indicates strong agreement between predictions and true labels, beyond what is expected by chance, and suggests the model handles class imbalance well.

  3. Sensitivity: The sensitivity for “vanilladot” is 99.95%, indicating that the model is excellent at identifying the positive class (loans likely to be repaid). This is critical in scenarios where minimizing missed positive cases is important.

  4. Simplicity and Efficiency: Linear kernels are computationally less expensive compared to more complex kernels like “rbfdot” or “polydot,” making them a more efficient choice when they perform equally well or better.

Once with the kernel chosen we can proceed to train and test the model. The confusion matrix for the Support Vector Machine (SVM) model with a linear kernel (vanilladot) provides the following insights:

  1. Accuracy: The model achieved an accuracy of 98.29%, demonstrating excellent overall performance in predicting loan repayment statuses. This high accuracy indicates the linear kernel is well-suited for this dataset.

  2. Kappa: The Kappa statistic is 0.8213, reflecting strong agreement between predictions and actual outcomes, beyond what would occur by chance. This highlights the model’s reliability in handling imbalanced classes.

  3. Sensitivity: The sensitivity is 99.95%, indicating that the SVM is nearly perfect at identifying loans that will be repaid (positive class).

  4. Specificity: The specificity is 71.56%, meaning the model performs moderately well at identifying loans that will default (negative class). While specificity is lower than sensitivity, it is sufficient given the strong overall performance.

  5. Positive Predictive Value (PPV): The PPV is 98.26%, showing that when the model predicts a loan will be repaid, it is correct the vast majority of the time. This high precision is valuable for reducing the risk of approving potentially defaulted loans.

  6. Balanced Accuracy: The balanced accuracy, which averages sensitivity and specificity, is 85.75%, reflecting the model’s robustness across both classes.

The SVM model with the linear kernel demonstrates outstanding performance, particularly in accuracy and sensitivity, making it a reliable tool for predicting loan repayment outcomes. While the specificity could be improved to better detect defaulted loans, the model strikes a good balance between identifying repaid loans and minimizing false positives.

f. Decision Tree Model

A Decision Tree is a machine learning model that predicts outcomes by recursively splitting the dataset into subsets based on feature values. It starts with a root node representing the entire dataset, splits into decision nodes based on the most significant features, and ends at leaf nodes, which represent the final predictions or outcomes. Decision trees are widely used for classification and regression tasks due to their simplicity, interpretability, and ability to model complex, non-linear relationships.

#plot(dt)

prediction_dt <- predict(dt, newdata = test_encoded)

                         as.factor(test_encoded$y), 
                         positive = "1")

  3. Sensitivity: The sensitivity is 99.96%, showing that the model is nearly perfect at identifying loans likely to be repaid (positive class). This minimizes false negatives, which is critical for ensuring reliable predictions of repaid loans.

  4. Specificity: The specificity is 70.79%, indicating moderate success in identifying loans that will default (negative class). While specificity is lower than sensitivity, it is sufficient given the Decision Tree’s overall strong performance.

While the specificity could be improved to better identify defaulted loans, the model strikes a strong balance between minimizing false positives and achieving high accuracy. In order to try and improve the specificity, as it is in our business interest to reduce false positives, we will apply a cost matrix to the model.

Decision tree with cost matrix

The cost matrix is designed to adjust penalization weights for false positives and false negatives, prioritizing the reduction of the most critical error type. In this case, we aim to minimize false positives—instances where the model predicts a loan will be repaid, but it defaults. To achieve this, we apply a cost matrix that penalizes false positives 6 times more than false negatives, aligning the model with practical financial priorities.

cost_matrix <- matrix(c(0, 1,
                        6, 0),
                      nrow = 2,
                      byrow = TRUE)

rownames(cost_matrix) <- colnames(cost_matrix) <- c("0", "1")

dt2 <- C5.0(as.factor(y) ~ ., data = train_encoded, costs = cost_matrix)
#plot(dt2)

prediction_dt2 <- predict(dt2, newdata = test_encoded)

cm_dt2 <- confusionMatrix(as.factor(prediction_dt2), as.factor(test_encoded$y), positive = "1")
cm_dt2

g. Random Forest Model

A Random Forest model is an ensemble machine learning algorithm used for classification and regression tasks. It works by building multiple decision trees during training and aggregating their predictions to make a final decision. Each tree is trained on a random subset of the data and a random selection of features, introducing diversity among the trees and reducing the risk of overfitting. For classification, the model predicts the class with the majority vote from all trees, while for regression, it averages their outputs. Random Forests are highly effective for handling large datasets, managing missing data, and capturing non-linear relationships, making them versatile and robust for various predictive modeling tasks.

set.seed(12345)
model_rf <- randomForest(as.factor(y) ~ ., data = train_encoded, ntree=100)
#plot(model_rf)

prediction_rf <- predict(model_rf, newdata = test_encoded)

cm_rf <- confusionMatrix(as.factor(prediction_rf),
                as.factor(test_encoded$y),
                positive="1")

h. XGBoost Model

XGBoost (Extreme Gradient Boosting) is a powerful and scalable machine learning algorithm based on decision tree ensembles, designed for classification and regression tasks. It uses a gradient boosting framework, where models are built sequentially, and each new model corrects the errors of its predecessor. XGBoost stands out for its efficiency, regularization techniques to reduce overfitting, and ability to handle missing data. It supports parallel processing and tree pruning, making it computationally efficient even with large datasets. Its adaptability to handle non-linear relationships and high-dimensional data makes it a top choice for complex predictive modeling tasks, often delivering superior performance in competitions and real-world applications.

set.seed(12345)
labels <- train_encoded[, y_col]

model_xgb <- xgboost(data = as.matrix(train_encoded[, -y_col]),
                    label = as.matrix(labels),
                    nrounds = 100,
                    objective = "binary:logistic",
                    verbose = 0)

prediction_xgb <- predict(model_xgb, as.matrix(test_encoded[, -y_col]))
binary_prediction_xgb <- ifelse(prediction_xgb > 0.5, 1, 0)


cm_xgb <- confusionMatrix(
  as.factor(binary_prediction_xgb),
  as.factor(test_encoded[, y_col]), 
  positive="1"
)

i. Stacked Model

Business Note: After developing and training seven individual models, we will combine their strengths by creating a stacked model. This approach leverages the predictions from all the models to build a final, more robust model that capitalizes on the unique strengths of each. By combining insights from multiple algorithms, the stacked model aims to improve prediction accuracy and reliability, providing a comprehensive solution for identifying loan repayment outcomes. This method ensures a more confident and data-driven approach to decision-making.

The first step in building a stacked model is to consolidate all predictions from the individual models into a single dataset. This dataset will serve as the input for the stacked model, allowing it to analyze and learn from the combined outputs of the base models. Alongside the predictions, it is essential to include the target variable from the test dataset, as this provides the ground truth needed for training and evaluating the stacked model. By unifying the predictions and the target variable, we create a comprehensive dataset that captures the strengths and weaknesses of each individual model, enabling the stacked model to make more accurate and reliable predictions. The code below demonstrates how this process is implemented:

response <- test_data$y
all_predictions <- data.frame(lr = binary_prediction_lr, 
                              knn = prediction_knn, 
                              ann = binary_prediction_ann, 
                              svm = prediction_svm, 
                              dt = prediction_dt,
                              rf = prediction_rf,
                              xgb = binary_prediction_xgb, 
                              response)
#str(all_predictions)

# Converting all into factors
all_predictions$lr <- as.factor(all_predictions$lr)
all_predictions$ann <- as.factor(all_predictions$ann)
all_predictions$xgb <- as.factor(all_predictions$xgb)
all_predictions$response <- as.factor(all_predictions$response)

Once the new dataset is created, the next step is to split it into training and testing subsets. This follows the same concept as the earlier data preparation, where the training subset is used to develop the stacked model, and the testing subset is reserved for evaluating its performance. By maintaining this separation, we ensure that the stacked model is validated on unseen data, providing an unbiased assessment of its predictive capabilities.

The training subset will include the predictions from the base models and the target variable, enabling the stacked model to learn how to best combine the individual predictions. The testing subset will then be used to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of the stacked model, ensuring its readiness for practical application. The code below demonstrates this process:

test_rate <- 0.5
set.seed(123)

test_prediction_rows <- sample(1:nrow(all_predictions), test_rate*nrow(all_predictions))
train_predictions <- all_predictions[-test_prediction_rows, ]
test_predictions <- all_predictions[test_prediction_rows, ]

Now, we proceed to create the stacked model, which is built as a decision tree applied to the dataset containing all the predictions from the individual models. The stacked model leverages the combined predictions of these models to make a final decision, improving overall predictive performance. By using a decision tree, the stacked model learns to identify patterns in how the base model predictions interact and which combinations are most indicative of the target outcome.

The decision tree serves as a meta-model, optimizing the strengths of the individual models and minimizing their weaknesses. This approach ensures that the final predictions are more robust and accurate, as they are derived from the collective insights of all the base models. The code snippet below illustrates the creation of the stacked model.

stack_model <- C5.0(as.factor(response) ~ ., data = train_predictions)
#plot(stack_model)

prediction_stack <- predict(stack_model, newdata = test_predictions)

cm_stack <- confusionMatrix(as.factor(prediction_stack),
                            as.factor(test_predictions$response),
                            positive="1")
cm_stack

  1. Accuracy: The stacked model achieved an accuracy of 98.33%, demonstrating excellent overall performance in predicting loan repayment outcomes. This high accuracy highlights the effectiveness of combining multiple model predictions into a single, cohesive solution.

  2. Kappa: The Kappa statistic is 0.8272, indicating strong agreement between the model’s predictions and actual outcomes, beyond chance. This suggests that the stacked model handles class imbalances effectively.

  3. Sensitivity: The sensitivity is 99.97%, meaning the model is almost perfect at identifying loans that will be repaid (positive class). This ensures minimal false negatives, a critical factor for predicting repaid loans accurately.

  4. Specificity: The specificity is 72.16%, indicating moderate performance in identifying defaulted loans (negative class). While lower than sensitivity, this is balanced by the model’s overall strength in classifying the positive class.

  5. Positive Predictive Value (PPV): The PPV is 98.29%, demonstrating that the model is highly reliable when predicting loans that will be repaid. This precision is crucial for reducing risks associated with misclassified defaulted loans.

  6. Balanced Accuracy: The balanced accuracy, which averages sensitivity and specificity, is 86.06%, reflecting robust overall performance across both classes.

The stacked model effectively combines the strengths of the individual base models, resulting in exceptional accuracy, sensitivity, and precision. While specificity could still be improved, the balanced accuracy indicates that the model performs well across both classes. By leveraging the insights from all the base models, the stacked model provides a highly reliable and comprehensive solution for predicting loan repayment outcomes. This approach ensures informed and confident decision-making, making it a valuable asset for the business.

To enhance the specificity of our final stacked model, which is crucial for our business purpose, we will implement a cost matrix to assign greater penalties to false positives. By doing so, the model will prioritize minimizing the misclassification of defaulted loans (negative class), thus improving its ability to correctly identify them.

This approach aligns with the strategy used previously for the decision tree model, where a cost matrix was applied to adjust the model’s focus based on business needs. The cost matrix ensures that the model’s predictions better reflect the practical implications of misclassifications, especially in scenarios where avoiding false positives is as important as achieving high overall accuracy.

The updated model with the cost matrix will provide a more balanced performance, ensuring it meets both operational and business objectives effectively.

cost_matrix <- matrix(c(0, 1,   
                       50, 0),  
                       nrow = 2,
                       byrow = TRUE)
rownames(cost_matrix) <- colnames(cost_matrix) <- c("0", "1")

stack2_model <- C5.0(as.factor(response) ~ ., data = train_predictions, costs = cost_matrix)

prediction_stack2 <- predict(stack2_model, newdata = test_predictions)

cm_stack2 <- confusionMatrix(as.factor(prediction_stack2),
                             as.factor(test_predictions$response),
                             positive="1")
cm_stack2

After applying a cost matrix to penalize false positives more heavily, the updated stacked model provides the following insights:

  1. Accuracy: The model achieved an accuracy of 98.29%, maintaining excellent overall performance. The slight reduction compared to the previous stacked model reflects the trade-off introduced by prioritizing specificity.

  2. Kappa: The Kappa statistic is 0.8253, indicating strong agreement between predictions and actual outcomes, beyond chance. This suggests the model continues to handle class imbalance effectively, even with the adjusted cost matrix.

  3. Sensitivity: The sensitivity is 99.87%, showing that the model remains highly effective at identifying loans that will be repaid (positive class). This ensures that very few repaid loans are misclassified as defaulted.

  4. Specificity: The specificity improved to 73.01%, reflecting a stronger ability to identify defaulted loans (negative class). This improvement is directly attributable to the cost matrix, which penalizes false positives more heavily.

  5. Positive Predictive Value (PPV): The PPV is 98.34%, demonstrating that the model is still highly reliable when predicting loans that will be repaid. This high precision ensures confident predictions for the majority class.

  6. Balanced Accuracy: The balanced accuracy, which averages sensitivity and specificity, is 86.44%, representing a slight improvement and reflecting better performance across both classes.

The introduction of the cost matrix successfully improved the model’s specificity, enhancing its ability to detect defaulted loans while maintaining strong sensitivity and accuracy. This adjustment aligns the model more closely with the business goal of minimizing false positives, ensuring a balanced and effective predictive solution. The updated stacked model provides greater reliability in identifying defaulted loans, making it an even more valuable tool for informed decision-making.

j. Comparison of the metrics from all models

With all the models built, trained, and tested, we compiled their key performance metrics — Accuracy, Specificity, Sensitivity, and Kappa — into a single table for comparison. This allows us to evaluate how each model performs across these metrics and identify their strengths and weaknesses. Below is the table summarizing the results:

##                 Model  Accuracy Specificity Sensitivity     Kappa
## 1 Logistic Regression 0.9756383   0.6767591   0.9942001 0.7520176
## 2                 KNN 0.9302813   0.2703625   0.9712651 0.2762046
## 3                 ANN 0.9839168   0.9997616   0.7287846 0.8329918
## 4      Vanilladot SVM 0.9828695   0.7155650   0.9994703 0.8212997
## 5       Decision Tree 0.9588819   0.7547974   0.9715565 0.6604485
## 6       Random Forest 0.9825703   0.7031983   0.9999205 0.8162367
## 7            XG Boost 0.9833932   0.7240938   0.9994968 0.8275149
## 8   Final Stack Model 0.9551666   0.7710197   0.9660399 0.6338350

In the given business scenario, where recognizing false positives (individuals predicted to repay loans but who actually default) is critical, Specificity becomes the key metric. This is because Specificity measures the model’s ability to correctly identify the negative class (defaulted loans), thereby minimizing false positives.

From the table, here are the insights:

  1. Logistic Regression performs well overall but has lower Specificity, meaning it struggles to identify defaulted loans, leading to more false positives.

  2. KNN has the lowest Specificity, making it unsuitable for this business context despite its decent Sensitivity. It would result in excessive false positives.

  3. ANN excels in Specificity, nearly perfect at identifying defaulted loans, but has low Sensitivity, which might result in overlooking some repayable loans.

  4. SVM balances Sensitivity and Specificity, with reasonable performance in identifying defaulted loans while maintaining excellent accuracy and Sensitivity.

  5. Decision Tree performs relatively well in Specificity, striking a balance between recognizing defaulted loans and maintaining good overall performance.

  6. Random Forest delivers strong Sensitivity but moderate Specificity, making it less ideal for minimizing false positives in this context.

  7. XGBoost strikes a good balance, with improved Specificity and high Sensitivity, making it a solid choice for this business scenario.

  8. The Stacked Model, incorporating insights from all models, offers a balanced approach. Its improved Specificity and strong Sensitivity make it particularly suited for the business objective.

Recommendation:

For the given business goal of reducing false positives (individuals predicted to repay loans but who actually default) is critical. Therefore, Specificity becomes the key metric. This is because Specificity measures the model’s ability to correctly identify the negative class (defaulted loans), thereby minimizing false positives.

  • ANN is the best at minimizing false positives due to its nearly perfect Specificity. However, its low Sensitivity might not generalize well across all scenarios.

  • The Final Stacked Model emerges as the best compromise, offering a strong balance between Specificity (77.10%) and Sensitivity (95.51%). It effectively identifies defaulted loans while maintaining overall accuracy and reliability.

Thus, the Final Stacked Model is the recommended choice, aligning well with the business priorities of reducing false positives while ensuring robust overall performance.

a. Business Case Conclusion:

Before Applying the Model:

Prior to using the model, total losses accounted for 10.12% of total revenue, reflecting a significant portion of loans that resulted in financial losses. Consequently, total profits represented 89.88% of total revenue, indicating profitability but leaving room for improvement due to the impact of defaulted loans.

After Applying the Model:

With the predictive model implemented, total losses decreased to 7.76% of total revenue, demonstrating a substantial reduction in financial losses by identifying and avoiding high-risk loans. Simultaneously, total profit increased to 92.24% of total revenue, highlighting an improvement in profitability as a result of more informed loan approval decisions.

Key Insights:

  1. Reduction in Losses: The model reduced losses by 2.36 percentage points (from 10.12% to 7.76%), showcasing its effectiveness in minimizing exposure to default risks. While this percentage change might not initially appear significant, 2.36% of the overall revenue accounts to 3.912,393.604 dollars.This financial impact highlights the meaningful contribution of the predictive model in improving the company’s bottom line.

  2. Increase in Profitability: Profitability improved by 2.36 percentage points (from 89.88% to 92.24%), reflecting the financial benefits of prioritizing loans with higher likelihoods of repayment.

  3. Enhanced Risk Management: The predictive model successfully improved the balance between risk and reward by reducing the proportion of loans that result in losses while maintaining a high level of revenue generation.

The comparison underscores the financial advantages of implementing the predictive model. By leveraging its ability to filter high-risk loans, the company achieves a more optimized lending strategy, reducing losses and enhancing overall profitability. This demonstrates the model’s strategic value in improving the company’s financial outcomes and risk management practices.


b. Lessons Learned and Improvement Points

Throughout this project, we encountered numerous decision points that involved meaningful trade-offs and required careful consideration. For example, determining whether to balance the dataset or deciding on the train/test split ratio were practical challenges that sparked valuable discussions. These decisions highlighted an essential aspect of data science: even in a mathematically precise and seemingly objective field, there are no universally “correct” answers. Instead, each decision depends on the context, objectives, and constraints of the project. Reflecting on these trade-offs underscored the importance of aligning technical choices with real-world implications and business goals.

Regarding areas for improvement, the primary limitation we faced was computational power. The dataset was exceptionally large, providing an opportunity to develop highly accurate and complex models. However, the lack of sufficient computational resources constrained our ability to explore more sophisticated approaches. For instance, it would have been valuable to implement a stepwise logistic regression or train a deeper Artificial Neural Network (ANN) with additional layers and neurons. These methods could have potentially yielded even better results but were beyond our computational capacity.
